title: Introduction to Derivative-Free Optimization — table of contents (Conn, Scheinberg, Vicente; SIAM MPS-SIAM Series on Optimization 8, 2009)
contribution: The authors' own map of DFO in 2009, read as a table of contents (joint voice). Chapter 1 covers why DFO, examples, limitations and how DF algorithms should work. Part I (about 100 pp.) gives sampling and modeling tools: positive spanning sets, linear, interpolation, regression and underdetermined models, poisedness, and ensuring well poisedness. Part II (about 114 pp.) gives directional and simplicial direct search, simplex-derivative line search, and derivative-free trust-region frameworks and practical methods. Part III reviews surrogates and constrained, global and mixed-integer extensions, followed by a software appendix. No title mentions complexity, rates, stochastic, multiobjective or benchmarking (pp. 1-3).
problem_entry: Enters through why and when before any tool: sections on why DFO, examples where derivatives are unavailable, limitations of DFO, and 'How derivative-free algorithms should work' (Ch. 1, sections 1.1-1.4, p. 1; title only).
key_idea: Tools first, algorithms second, extensions last. Part I builds sample-set geometry and model quality for both families, opening with the direct-search tools (positive spanning sets; gradient estimates used in direct search). Part II gives each family a chapter: two for direct search, one for line search, two for trust region (framework, then named methods). Constraints, surrogates, global and mixed-integer problems are only reviewed (pp. 1-3).
assumptions: Not stated in a TOC. Title-level scope: nonsmooth only in direct search (7.4), noise only in simplex-derivative line search (9.3), second-order results only for trust regions (10.5-10.6) (pp. 2-3).
proof_devices: Convergence titles are all 'Global convergence ...' (7.3, 7.4, 9.2, 10.4, 10.6); no title on rates, complexity or evaluation counts (pp. 1-3; title only)
Error bounds titled for linear interpolation and regression (2.4) and condition number as a measure of well poisedness (3.4, 4.4) (pp. 1-2; title only)
experiments: n/a. No section on comparisons, test sets or profiles; only an appendix 'Software for derivative-free optimization' (book p. 251) (p. 3).
positioning: Others' methods appear as section titles (MADS 7.6, Nelder-Mead 8.1-8.3, implicit filtering 9.4, the 'DFO' approach 11.2, Powell's methods 11.3, wedge methods 11.4). Globalization options sit side by side in Ch. 7: simple decrease with integer lattices (7.5), MADS (7.6), imposing sufficient decrease (7.7) (pp. 2-3; title only).
writing: Question-style section titles in Ch. 1 (p. 1). Exercises close every chapter except Chs. 1, 11, 13, and notes and references close Chs. 4-11 (pp. 1-3). Simplest instance before framework (coordinate search 7.1 before 7.2), and framework chapter before named-methods chapter (Ch. 10 then Ch. 11) (pp. 2-3). The longest section by page span is the globally convergent Nelder-Mead variant (8.3, book pp. 149-160) and the longest chapter is Ch. 10 (34 pp.) (pp. 2-3).
limits_future: Left out or kept short: complexity or rates; multiobjective, stochastic, probabilistic or randomized titles; constraints, global and mixed-integer problems only in review (Ch. 13, 13.3); no one-dimensional DF methods (pp. 1-3; the reviewer B005 p. 3 names the last gap). A limitations section sits in the introduction (1.3, p. 1). The chapters themselves are not read.

method_links.note: Title only. Ch. 7 presents the directional framework and then three globalization options, including 'Imposing sufficient decrease' (7.7) next to integer lattices (7.5) and MADS (7.6). So the co-authored book taught sufficient decrease as one option in 2009, while SKILL.md dates the switch in Vicente's own papers to 2013 [S023 p. 4]; the dating of the papers stands. Heuristics given convergence theory get their own sections: the globally convergent Nelder-Mead variant (8.3, the book's longest section), implicit filtering (9.4), and rigorous frameworks for surrogates (12.2).
Era, title only: analysis titles are 'Global convergence ...'; no title mentions complexity, rates or evaluation counts. The complexity line starts after the book [S023].

Deterministic baseline, title only: 'Fully linear and fully quadratic models' (6.1) and 'Conditions on the trust-region models' (10.2) name the model-quality notion later relaxed probabilistically [S014]; 'Analysis for noise' (9.3) is the only noise title; nothing probabilistic.
Weak, title only: the nonsmooth case is a section of the same direct-search chapter (7.4); constrained and other extensions are reviewed per framework (13.1-13.2), not as new algorithm families.
Genre: a software appendix (book p. 251), but no section on collections, comparisons or profiles.
Title level, joint authors: 'Limitations of derivative-free optimization' is a section of the introduction (1.3), before the summary of the book.

Supports 'The co-authored book and geometry papers certify models deterministically': a whole chapter on ensuring well poisedness, with Lagrange-polynomial and pivotal algorithms and practical considerations (6.2-6.4). Title only.

title: Errata to Introduction to Derivative-Free Optimization (05/17/2015)
contribution: Author-maintained errata for the first printing: 18 items located by book page and line, most with the old text and a corrected version (items 3, 11, 15 give no old text; item 14 is a deletion; item 15 gives no line). By kind: theorem statement and proof 4 (the Theorem 2.13 / regression simplex gradient cluster, book pp. 29-34), constants 6 (Lambda values of the poisedness examples; kappa constants of the quadratic regression bound), example data and regions 2, statement precision 5, index typo 1. Part I carries 13 of 18 items; none fall in Chs. 8-11. The list closes by thanking Griewank, Hare, Le Digabel and Vaz by name (pp. 1-3).
problem_entry: Correct the first printing: items are located by page and line, and most quote the wrong text before a 'Corrected version' (items 3, 11, 15 give no old text; item 14 is a deletion; item 15 gives no line) (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: A self-correction record with dependants chased. The Theorem 2.13 fix carries through to the p. 33 remark, the 'obvious' claim and Exercise 10 (items 3-6), and the Lambda-value fixes carry through to the sentence explaining the old value (items 13-14). The superseded statement's valid case is kept on record (pp. 1-3).
assumptions: Scope note: the old Theorem 2.13 would be valid for the model m(y) = f(y0) + (y - y0)^T g, whose g is the regression simplex gradient. The corrected theorem covers the general linear regression model with a free constant term. The theorem's Assumption 2.2 is named, but its content is not in the list (pp. 1-2).
proof_devices: replacement proof of Theorem 2.13: assume y0 = 0 (argument at the end of the proof of Thm 3.16); M = [1 0; e L] and its scaled version; Taylor data give M[f(y0); grad f(y0)] - f(Y) = r with |r_i| <= (nu/2)Delta^2; coefficient error = M^dagger r with the Moore-Penrose left inverse (M^T M)^-1 M^T; scaling M^dagger = diag(1, (1/Delta)I) Mhat^dagger (new (2.9), stated without proof; showing it and concluding is the rewritten Exercise 10, item 6, so the replacement is a proof outline); kappa_eg = nu(1 + p^{1/2}||Mhat^dagger||/2), kappa_ef = 2 kappa_eg + nu/2 (pp. 1-2, as extracted)

same device as the addendum B004 and the Taylor-subtraction plus Delta-scaling error bounds of [S010 pp. 12-16]; the 2008 regression bounds had been stated without proof as 'straightforward adaptations' [S020 pp. 14-16] (sequence only, no stated cause)
positioning: Credits four readers by name for pointing out errors: Andreas Griewank, Warren Hare, Sebastien Le Digabel, A. Ismael F. Vaz (p. 3). From the skill's records, not this text: Vaz is the PSwarm coauthor [S005] and Le Digabel a MADS-globalization coauthor with Audet and Dennis, so reports came from a coauthor and from the mesh school (inference).
writing: For most items the old text is quoted exactly and followed by 'Corrected version:', with page and line; negative line numbers count from below (p. 1). Items 3 and 11 give only the new text, item 14 only a deletion, item 15 neither line nor old text (pp. 1, 3). A failing passage is replaced whole, including a restated theorem (pp. 1-2). 'It is then obvious' becomes 'It can be proved using arguments already seen' (p. 2). No apology or hedging; one sentence of thanks (p. 3).
limits_future: Does not say how the errors arose or whether any later result used the old constants (pp. 1-3). Dated 05/17/2015, the list's revision date; when each item was first posted is not given (p. 1).

method_links.note: Step 5 'post errata' (joint authors): a dated per-printing list of 18 items located by page and line, most with old and corrected text (items 3, 11, 15 give no old text; item 14 is a deletion; item 15 gives no line). It is the first errata list actually read for the skill; the DMS errata remain uninspected.
The book's errata join the DMS errata cited as the evidenced norm.

A printed theorem (2.13) needed a new statement and a new proof outline, and printed constants needed recomputation (Lambda values, kappa constants). These are self-corrections, unlike the external counterexample the rule cites.

Post-publication form: the replacement keeps on record the model form under which the old Theorem 2.13 remains valid; item 2 names the failure mode ('trapped at a spurious minimizer') instead of 'failed'.

Theorem 2.13 was stated for the general linear regression model but, as printed, holds for the model anchored at f(y0). This is a scope error found and fixed by the authors themselves, not an edge-of-regularity conclusion refuted by others (cf. the 2024 counterexample to [S024]).
The book's errata are now read; the DMS errata and the solver code are still not.

transferable: For each erratum give page and line and, where the change is local, the exact wrong text next to the corrected text; one list per printing (pp. 1-3).

Least-squares model error device: write the Taylor coefficients as solving the regression system up to a residual r, so the coefficient error is M^dagger r. Then factor the Delta-powers out by scaling to the unit ball, and the constant is the norm of the scaled pseudo-inverse (pp. 1-2).

title: Derivation of Error Bounds for Quadratic Regression (01/27/2011) — addendum to Introduction to Derivative-Free Optimization
contribution: A two-page author addendum that derives the error bounds of the book's Theorem 4.13 for quadratic regression models, based on the condition number of the scaled regression matrix. It gives explicit Hessian, gradient and function-value constants with dimension factors n^{1/2} and p-bar^{1/2} (p-bar = n(n + 1)/2), matching in form the corrected constants of erratum item 11 (pp. 1-2; B002 p. 3).
problem_entry: One sentence: the bounds 'given in Theorem 4.13, can be derived as follows' (p. 1). The note does not say why it was posted separately. Its constants have the form of the corrected kappa constants in the errata, so it works as the derivation behind a posted correction (inference) (pp. 1-2; B002 p. 3).
key_idea: Treat the Taylor coefficients at y0 as an exact least-squares solution up to a residual, so the coefficient error equals M^dagger r. Diagonal scaling to a sample set in the unit ball pulls out the Delta-powers and leaves the conditioning of the scaled matrix as the constant (pp. 1-2).
assumptions: y0 = 0 without loss of generality (argument at the end of the proof of Thm 3.16). Model m(y) = c + g^T y + (1/2) y^T H y with the canonical basis of (3.1). Hessian of f Lipschitz with constant nu_2. M of full column rank, so M^dagger = (M^T M)^-1 M^T. Scaled sample set in B(0;1) (p. 1).
proof_devices: residual system M[f(y0); grad f(y0); vec(Hess f(y0))] - f(Y) = r with |r_i| bounded by a constant times Delta^3 (the extraction prints the factor as (nu/2)Delta^3), and coefficient error = M^dagger r, display (0.1) (p. 1)
Hessian block bound p-bar^{1/2}(nu_2/2)||M^dagger||Delta, times sqrt(2) from vec to matrix (0.3); plus nu_2 Delta to move from y0 to y (pp. 1-2)

gradient block n^{1/2}(nu_2/2)||M^dagger||Delta^2 (0.4); Taylor with a mean-value point t in (0,1), adding and subtracting Hess f(y0) y, gives (nu_2 + ((n^{1/2} + sqrt(2) p-bar^{1/2})/2) nu_2 ||M^dagger||) Delta^2 (p. 2)
function values (nu_2/2 + (1/2 + n^{1/2}/2 + sqrt(2) p-bar^{1/2}/4) nu_2 ||M^dagger||) Delta^3 (p. 2)
same Moore-Penrose footnote, word for word, as the errata's replacement proof of Theorem 2.13 (p. 1; B002 p. 1); same device as [S010 pp. 12-16]
positioning: Cites only the book's own items (Theorem 3.16, basis (3.1), Theorem 4.13); no outside references (p. 1). The 2008 regression paper had stated its regression bounds without proof [S020 pp. 14-16].
writing: Two pages of derivation with numbered displays (0.1)-(0.4) and one footnote. No prose motivation beyond the first sentence, and no restatement of the theorem (pp. 1-2).
limits_future: No discussion of whether the constants are sharp; the theorem is not restated (pp. 1-2).

method_links.note: Post-publication support (joint authors): a dated derivation posted with the book's material, with constants matching the corrected ones in the errata.
Explicit constants with dimension factors, but for approximation error, not evaluation counts (as for [S010]).
Deterministic model certification: the accuracy constant is the norm of the scaled regression matrix's pseudo-inverse, so sample-set geometry decides model accuracy.
For this one theorem the posted derivation and the corrected constants agree in form as extracted; they were not re-derived here, so the caution stands.

title: Review of Introduction to Derivative-Free Optimization (Mathematics of Computation 79(271), 2010)
contribution: External review by J. L. Nazareth (University of Washington), in the reviewer's voice only. He calls the book a state-of-the-art monograph on smooth, unconstrained problems with up to about a hundred variables. Part I is a well-presented mathematical toolkit, and trust-region model-based methods are 'the centerpiece'. Weaknesses: theory-only exercises, atypical introductory examples, few numerical illustrations and no implementation details, no one-dimensional methods, and the DFO/nondifferentiable intersection not adequately addressed. He files it under the 'theoretical algorithmic science mode' of his own framework (pp. 1-3).
problem_entry: Reviewer's framing: problems 'benign' (smooth, unconstrained, 'say up to a hundred' variables) yet 'extremely challenging' because derivatives are unavailable and evaluations are expensive or noisy; Nelder-Mead was the old 'standard workhorse' whose mid-nineties theory spurred renewed research (p. 1).
key_idea: Reviewer's reading: DF methods as 'sampling the objective function at several points, sufficiently spaced apart' (book p. 57, quoted) and 'gradient-related'. Part I is the machinery. In Part II, direct search is described as search step, poll with a positive basis and parameter update; implicit filtering is 'sandwiched in between'; the trust-region frameworks with first- and second-order convergence are the centerpiece, with the DFO approach, Powell's methods and wedge methods. Part III is brief, and the software appendix is useful (pp. 1-2).
assumptions: Reviewer's scope statement: reasonably smooth, unconstrained, relatively few variables; convergence relies on smoothness assumptions (p. 1).
experiments: Peer view: 'few numerical illustrations' (compared with Kelley) and 'no implementational details'; the focus is not on 'algorithmic engineering' (p. 3).
positioning: Reviewer places the book against Nelder-Mead history (p. 1), Kelley 1999 (numerics), Brent 1973 (one-dimensional methods), Numerical Recipes (software developers) and his own 2006 SIAM News article on algorithmic science and engineering, whose lens is his, not the authors' (p. 3).
writing: Reviewer's review: summary by part, then weaknesses, then a conclusion 'on a more personal note'. Praise is specific ('nicely organized and well presented', p. 2; 'gracefully-written, well-organized, and timely', p. 3), and each criticism comes with a pointer (Kelley, Brent, Rademacher) (pp. 1-3). The editorial 'we' belongs to a single signed reviewer (pp. 1, 3).
limits_future: Per the reviewer: exercises mostly elaborations of theory, diminishing use for an introductory course (p. 2); introductory examples 'atypical of applications' in the book's own words (book p. 3, quoted; p. 2); few numerics, no implementation details; no one-dimensional methods; the DFO/nondifferentiable intersection not adequately addressed (p. 3).

method_links.note: Genre, peer view: few numerical illustrations and no implementation details, only a software appendix the reviewer calls useful; fits Method 5's 'no numerics in theory-first papers' genre variant.

Peer view of the co-authored book: the directional iteration read as search step + poll with positive basis + parameter update; Nelder-Mead 'recent modifications that are designed to guarantee convergence'.

method_links.method: Inner Tension: Direct-search skeleton vs borrowed derivatives and models
method_links.note: The reviewer calls the trust-region model-based methods the book's 'centerpiece', while Vicente's own algorithm papers keep models in the search step; the joint book leans model-based (Conn lens).

Scope, peer view: the book's methods are smooth and 'gradient-related', and the nondifferentiable intersection is a named gap. Vicente's nonsmooth and discontinuous direct-search papers run 2008-2013 [S030; S024; S034]; chronology only, no source links them to the review.

The preface's aims (book pp. xi-xii), quoted by the reviewer, tie convergence theory to algorithm design and to 'what kind of success one can expect and where'. They are second-hand and joint, so they add no own-words statement by Vicente.

transferable: Integrate exercises into the text, or make them practical rather than elaborations of theory (p. 2).
Choose introductory examples typical of applications, or say plainly they are not; the book said so and the reviewer still counted it against the book (p. 2).
Add numerical illustrations and implementation details (p. 3).
Check the neighbouring classes readers will ask about: one-dimensional methods, nonsmooth problems (p. 3).
coauthors: none (external review by J. L. Nazareth, University of Washington; not a Vicente work)

quotes.text: The discussion of the other main class of methods—trust-region algorithms based on derivative-free linear and quadratic models—is the centerpiece of the monograph.
The important intersection between derivative-free optimization and non-differentiable optimization is not adequately addressed.

title: Review of Introduction to Derivative-Free Optimization (SIAM Review book reviews)
contribution: External review by Dominique Orban (Ecole Polytechnique de Montreal), in the reviewer's voice only; SIAM Review 53(2), 2011, pp. 395-396 (year and issue from Crossref: the Book Reviews section of 53(2), online 5 May 2011, pp. 375-405, DOI 10.1137/SIREAD000053000002000375000001; the text gives none, and the batch first listed 2010). Orban predicts the book will be the de facto authoritative text. He praises its treatment of both families' limitations and the clarity of Part I, and suggests a course of cursory Part I, then Part II. Weaknesses: theory exercises, few examples, the only method comparison in the introduction (comparison is, per the authors, not an objective), mostly research-grade software; he wishes for bare-bones implementations (pp. 1-2).
problem_entry: Opens with a verdict: 'bound to become the de facto authoritative text' on numerical methods for problems whose derivatives are unavailable, whether not known to exist or existing but unavailable (p. 1).
key_idea: Reviewer's reading. The introduction's first example is parameter tuning (his 'personal favorite'). Part I and Part II are separated so readers can start on algorithms after a cursory Part I. Part II has two frameworks: direct search (GPS, mesh-adaptive, convergent Nelder-Mead variants, the latter 'almost a simple and didactic illustration of the direct-search framework') and model-based (a simplex-gradient line-search variant of trust region; trust region). Part III covers constraints and surrogates, kept 'so as to retain their convergence properties' (pp. 1-2).
assumptions: Per the reviewer, in his paragraph on the trust-region model-based chapters: Lipschitz-continuous gradient or Hessian, and an interpolatory or least-squares model on a well-poised sample set; contrasted with the 30 nonsmooth pages of Conn-Gould-Toint's Trust-Region Methods (p. 2). Read as scoped to those chapters: the book also has a nonsmooth direct-search section (7.4, B001 p. 2).
experiments: Peer view: 'the only comparison between methods to be found in the book' is in the introduction; per the reviewer, the authors say comparing DF methods is intricate and not an objective of the book (his paraphrase; book wording not read). Most pointed-to software is 'research grade and not necessarily accessible to the nonexpert' (pp. 1-2).
positioning: Reviewer places the book beside Conn-Gould-Toint's Trust-Region Methods (same series, one common author), as 'one of the very few textbooks available on this topic', with the authors as 'central players in the field'. Surrogate vs model terminology: a surrogate as 'fortune teller' (p. 2).
writing: Reviewer's review: warm and specific, first person ('I particularly appreciated', 'In my opinion', 'a personal wish'); criticism framed as 'a respectable choice' plus a wish (pp. 1-2).
limits_future: Per the reviewer: exercises mostly extensions of theory, few examples, no hands-on implementations ('bare-bones implementations' wished for), mostly research-grade software (p. 2). Compared with B005: both flag theory exercises, few numerics or examples and weak software; they disagree on textbook use (Orban: appropriate for a graduate class, 'essential both as an introductory text and as a reference volume'; Nazareth: diminished for an introductory course) and on where the line search belongs (pp. 1-2; B005 pp. 2-3).

method_links.note: Peer view: the reviewer singles out the treatment of both families' limitations as the aspect he 'particularly appreciated'; matches the limitations section of the introduction (B001 p. 1).

Genre, peer view: the only method comparison is in the introduction; by the reviewer's account the authors say comparison is not an objective; software mostly research grade; implementations wished for. The authors' stance is second-hand.
Peer view: surrogates included in the Part II methods 'so as to retain their convergence properties'; Nelder-Mead presented as an illustration of the direct-search framework.

Peer view: in the trust-region model-based chapters, models rest on a well-poised sample set with Lipschitz gradient or Hessian assumptions, and states where derivative-free trust-region theory differs from the smooth one (deterministic model certification).
